english: moreover; on top of that; what's more
usage: and on top of that it even rained
The particle 까지 ('even') loves to sit on the added item, underlining that it's one burden too many
Frequently follows a -은/는데 clause that has already laid out the first reason
especially at a time like now
Stresses that the surrounding circumstances make the added fact land even harder
and on top of it I'm sick too
The 도 on the new clause signals 'this as well,' the natural partner of 더구나
examples: 비가 와요. 더구나 바람도 불어요.
It's raining. On top of that, the wind is blowing too.
Simple two-sentence stack; note 도 on the second, added point
그 식당은 비싸요. 더구나 맛도 별로였어요.
That restaurant is expensive. What's more, the food wasn't even good.
Everyday complaint that piles a second negative onto the first
초보자에게는 어려운 책인데, 더구나 분량까지 많아서 다 못 읽었어요.
It's a hard book for beginners, and on top of that it's so long that I couldn't finish it.
Real situation: 까지 marks the final straw that produced the outcome
nuance: 더구나 piles an extra fact on top of what you just said, and that extra fact almost always tips the situation further in one direction — usually worse ('and to make matters worse'). Its closest rivals are 게다가 and 더욱이: all three mean 'on top of that,' but 게다가 is the neutral everyday default that happily adds good or bad news, 더욱이 is the most bookish, and 더구나 sits between them, leaning emotional and feeling like the speaker is fed up. It habitually teams up with 도/까지 on the new clause (비도, 사람까지) and trails after a -는데 set-up. It is purely an adverb that opens or links a clause — never a noun. The English-speaker trap is reaching for 더구나 to tack a cheerful, neutral item onto a list ('I bought apples, and moreover bananas'); there 그리고 or 게다가 is right, because 더구나 quietly promises that the addition raises the stakes.

mistakes: Using 더구나 to add a positive or purely neutral item ('샀어요, 더구나 바나나도'): it implies the addition intensifies (usually worsens) the situation, so a flat list needs 그리고/게다가 instead.
Treating it as a noun or object ('더구나가 있어요'): it is an adverb that opens or links a clause, so it can never take 이/가 or 을/를.
Forgetting the 도/까지 partner: '비 왔어요. 더구나 추웠어요' feels bare — Koreans naturally say '더구나 춥기까지 했어요' so the 'one more thing' flavor is carried by the particle.

usage: Singles out one favorite member from a larger set you just named
Sits directly in front of an adjective to boost that one quality
The set phrase 그중에서도 ('even among those') often leads into 특히 to narrow down
특히나 is a slightly stronger, more colloquial variant of 특히
examples: 저는 과일을 좋아하는데, 특히 딸기를 제일 좋아해요.
I like fruit, and I especially like strawberries the most.
Simple: state the category, then 특히 zooms to one item
이번 시험은 특히 듣기 부분이 어려웠어요.
This time the exam was especially hard in the listening section.
Everyday: 특히 highlights which part stood out from the rest
주말에는 사람이 많은데, 특히 일요일 오후가 제일 붐벼요.
It's crowded on weekends, and Sunday afternoons in particular are the most packed.
Real situation: narrows a general statement down to the worst case
nuance: 특히 (Sino-Korean 特, 'special/distinct') points at one member of a group and says 'this one stands out from the rest' — exactly English 'especially' or 'in particular.' The word it constantly gets confused with is its sibling 특별히 (特別, 'special-distinct'): 특히 selects the most notable item from a set, while 특별히 says something was done in a special, deliberate way ('특별히 준비했어요' = I went out of my way to prepare it). Picture 특히 as a spotlight that picks one face out of a crowd, and 특별히 as the extra effort behind a gesture. 특히 naturally rides after a general statement and then pinpoints the exception, and it loves the lead-in 그중에서도. The classic English-speaker pitfall is using 특히 to mean 'I did it specially' — that intent meaning belongs to 특별히, not 특히.

mistakes: Confusing 특히 (singling out one from a group) with 특별히 (doing something in a special/deliberate way): '특히 준비했어요' wrongly says 'I prepared it, of all things,' when you mean '특별히 준비했어요' (I made special preparations).
Parking 특히 far from the item it highlights so the listener can't tell what is being singled out: keep it right next to that word — 특히 듣기가, not 특히 ... 듣기가 ... 어려웠어요 with words in between.
Trying to negate with 특히 ('not especially'): the idiomatic 'not particularly' uses 특별히 + 부정 (특별히 어렵지 않아요), so don't say '특히 어렵지 않아요.'

usage: States your dominant habit while leaving room for exceptions
Marks the place where something typically happens
Identifies the chief object, target, or ingredient
Often follows a time frame to describe what usually fills it
examples: 저는 주말에 주로 집에서 쉬어요.
On weekends I mostly rest at home.
Simple: 주로 describes the typical, default pattern
이 카페에는 주로 학생들이 와요.
Mostly students come to this cafe.
Everyday: marks the dominant kind of customer, not 'only'
점심은 주로 회사 근처에서 간단히 먹는 편이에요.
I usually eat lunch simply near the office.
Real situation: 주로 + -는 편이다 softens it to 'as a rule, tend to'
nuance: 주로 (Sino-Korean 主, 'main/principal') means 'mainly/mostly' and names the dominant case among several options, leaving the door open for exceptions. It overlaps with 보통 ('usually') and 대부분 ('for the most part'), but the dividing line is what each emphasizes: 보통 is about frequency over time, 대부분 is about proportion/quantity, and 주로 is about which option is the principal one ('주로 버스로 다녀요' = the bus is my main mode, though not the only one). It is the natural word for describing habits, typical locations, and the main type of thing involved. Crucially it is strictly an adverb here, not the noun 주류 ('the mainstream') that shares the 主 root. The English-speaker pitfall is letting 'mostly' slide into 'always': 주로 signals a strong tendency, so if you truly mean 100%, you need 항상 or 늘 instead.

mistakes: Using 주로 to mean 'absolutely always': it names a tendency, so for a no-exceptions claim use 항상/늘 — '저는 항상 집에서 쉬어요' is total, '주로' is just usual.
Confusing the adverb 주로 with the noun 주류 ('mainstream/alcoholic beverages'): here it can only modify a verb or adjective, never take a particle like 주로가.
Reaching for 주로 to talk about pure frequency ('I mostly go three times a week'): for counting how often, 보통 fits better, while 주로 is for which option dominates.

usage: Sits in front of an adjective to soften the claim against an unstated standard
Can name the yardstick explicitly with -에 비해
it's on the relatively small side
Often pairs with -은/는 편이다 to hedge an amount or degree
Modifies time words too: 'fairly recently, as these things go'
examples: 이 동네는 비교적 조용해요.
This neighborhood is relatively quiet.
Simple: hedges the claim against other areas you have in mind
오늘은 비교적 일이 적어서 일찍 퇴근했어요.
Today there was comparatively little work, so I left early.
Everyday: implies 'less than usual,' an implicit comparison to normal days
한국어 발음은 영어에 비해 비교적 규칙적이라서 배우기 쉬워요.
Korean pronunciation is relatively regular compared to English, so it's easy to learn.
Real situation: -에 비해 makes the standard explicit
nuance: 비교적 (Sino-Korean 比較的, literally '比較 comparison' + the 的 '-ish/in-the-manner-of' suffix) means 'relatively/comparatively' and tells the listener that the quality holds only against some standard, not in absolute terms. That hedge makes you sound careful and measured. Set it against 꽤 and 좀: 꽤 means 'quite/considerably' as a plain intensifier with no comparison built in, 좀 just means 'a bit,' while 비교적 specifically invokes a yardstick ('relative to other options'). Unlike 별로, it carries no negative bias — 비교적 can be relatively good or relatively bad. Because of the 的 suffix it stays adverbial and never conjugates: you cannot say 비교적이에요. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that — turning 'relative' into a predicate; in Korean 비교적 only modifies (비교적 쉬워요), and there should always be at least an implied point of comparison behind it.

Using it where there is genuinely nothing to compare against: 비교적 needs a baseline (even unspoken), so for a flat statement with no yardstick, plain 좀/꽤 is better.
Treating 비교적 as a strong intensifier like 'very': it actually tones a claim down to 'relatively,' so '비교적 어려워요' means moderately hard, not extremely hard — for 'very' use 아주/정말.

english: on the whole; generally; for the most part
usage: Extremely common in reviews and overall evaluations
Gives a big-picture verdict that tolerates minor exceptions
Smooths over small differences to state the overall impression
Often sets up a 'mostly good, with one caveat' structure
examples: 이 식당 음식은 대체로 맛있어요.
The food at this restaurant is generally good.
Simple: an overall verdict, not a claim about every dish
호텔은 대체로 깨끗했지만 와이파이가 좀 느렸어요.
The hotel was on the whole clean, though the Wi-Fi was a bit slow.
Everyday: -지만 carves out the one exception to the general impression
설문 결과를 보면 사람들은 대체로 새 정책에 찬성하는 것 같아요.
Looking at the survey, people seem to generally support the new policy.
Real situation: summarizes a broad trend across many responses
nuance: 대체로 (Sino-Korean 大體, 'the 大 large 體 body/substance' → the main gist) delivers an overall, big-picture judgment — 'on the whole' — while quietly admitting that small exceptions exist. It is the natural word for summaries and evaluations and sounds a touch analytical. Compare it with 주로 and 보통: 주로 picks the single dominant case ('주로 학생이 와요' = mainly students), whereas 대체로 averages over the whole situation to state a general tendency ('대체로 만족스러워요' = satisfied overall, weighing everything). It often pairs with -지만 to add the one caveat. Do not confuse 대체로 with the look-alike 대체 (= 도대체, 'on earth') used in exasperated questions like '대체 왜?' — same first syllable, unrelated meaning. The English-speaker pitfall is using 대체로 about a single concrete event ('today's lunch was generally good'); it describes overall tendencies across a set, so for one instance you would just say 맛있었어요.

Confusing it with 대체 (= 도대체, 'on earth/in the world') in questions: '대체 왜 그래요?' is exasperation, while 대체로 is 'on the whole' — same syllable, opposite job.
Swapping 대체로 and 주로 freely: 주로 names the dominant option, 대체로 gives an averaged overall verdict, so 'mainly students come' is 주로, while 'the service was good overall' is 대체로.

usage: States what is usually true as a rule or principle
A set lead-in that opens a broad generalization
The adjective form 일반적이다 modifies nouns directly
Frequently sets up a norm to be contrasted with exceptions
examples: 일반적으로 봄에는 날씨가 따뜻해요.
Generally, the weather is warm in spring.
Simple: states a rule-of-thumb truth
일반적으로 이런 증상은 며칠이면 좋아져요.
Generally, symptoms like these get better within a few days.
Everyday: gives a typical expectation, the explanatory register of a doctor or article
일반적으로 말하면, 경험이 많을수록 일이 수월해져요.
Generally speaking, the more experience you have, the easier the work becomes.
Real situation: 말하면 frames a broad principle before stating it
nuance: 일반적으로 (Sino-Korean 一般, 'one-kind' → ordinary/common, + 的 + the adverbial -으로) introduces a general rule or what is typically the case — 'in general,' 'typically.' It is noticeably more formal and explanatory than the everyday 보통, which is why it dominates writing, explanations, and academic-leaning speech, whereas 보통 fits casual chat ('보통 7시에 일어나요'). Think of 일반적으로 as the voice of a textbook or an expert stating a norm. Its built-in counterpart is 예외적으로 ('as an exception'), and the two often frame a rule-versus-exception contrast. The form matters: the adverbial -으로 is obligatory, so you cannot drop it and use bare 일반적 as an adverb (that stem only lives inside 일반적인 N or 일반적이다). The English-speaker pitfall is using this formal word for personal habits ('I generally wake at seven'); for your own routines 주로/보통 sound far more natural than 일반적으로.

Using formal 일반적으로 for personal habits ('저는 일반적으로 7시에 일어나요'): for your own routine 보통/주로 are natural, and 일반적으로 sounds like you're stating a societal law about yourself.
Forgetting it sets up a norm vs. exception: pairing it with a one-off surprise is odd, since 일반적으로 invites the implicit 'but sometimes 예외적으로…' frame.

usage: Common collocation: deliberately paying extra attention
there's nothing in particular I want to V
특별히 + negative is the idiomatic 'not really / nothing special'
특별히 = in a special way; 특히 = singled out from a group
examples: 오늘은 손님이 와서 특별히 음식을 많이 준비했어요.
We have guests today, so I specially prepared a lot of food.
Simple: emphasizes deliberate, beyond-the-usual effort
특별히 가고 싶은 곳은 없어요. 아무 데나 괜찮아요.
There's no place I particularly want to go. Anywhere is fine.
Everyday: the very common 특별히 + 없다 'nothing in particular' pattern
선생님이 저를 특별히 챙겨 주셔서 정말 감사했어요.
The teacher looked after me especially well, so I was really grateful.
Real situation: marks special, individualized treatment toward one person
nuance: 특별히 (Sino-Korean 特別, 'special-distinct') means doing or feeling something in a special, deliberate, out-of-the-ordinary way, and in negative sentences it softens into 'not particularly.' Its constant point of confusion is 특히 ('especially'): 특별히 is about the special manner or intent behind an action ('특별히 만들었어요' = I made it specially, with effort), while 특히 just selects the standout item from a set ('과일 중에 특히 딸기' = strawberries above the other fruits). A useful mental split: 특별히 answers 'in what way?' (specially), 특히 answers 'which one?' (that one). 특별히 strongly favors negative frames — 특별히 ~없어요/않아요 is the everyday way to say 'nothing in particular / not really.' The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: using 특별히 when you mean 'among these, especially X' (that's 특히), and forgetting that the most natural 'not especially' is precisely 특별히 + a negative, not 특히 + a negative.

Its constant point of confusion is 특히 ('especially'): 특별히 is about the special manner or intent behind an action ('특별히 만들었어요' = I made it specially, with effort), while 특히 just selects the standout item from a set ('과일 중에 특히 딸기' = strawberries above the other fruits). mistakes: Using 특별히 where you mean 'among these, especially X' ('과일 중에 특별히 딸기'): selecting one from a group is 특히 — 특별히 would imply the strawberry was treated in some special way.
Forgetting that 'not particularly / nothing in particular' is idiomatically 특별히 + negative: say '특별히 어렵지 않아요' / '특별히 없어요,' not 특히 어렵지 않아요.
Reading 특별히 as plain 'very': it means 'in a special/deliberate way,' so '특별히 비싸요' implies an unusual, pointed expensiveness, not a generic 'very expensive' (that's 아주 비싸요).

usage: The signature collocation — flags the single most important point
Adding -도 to 무엇보다 strengthens the 'above absolutely all' feel
A common lead-in that announces your key point
Stresses priority in both order and importance
examples: 건강이 무엇보다 중요해요.
Health is more important than anything.
Simple: the textbook 무엇보다 + 중요하다 pairing
여러 이유가 있지만, 무엇보다 가족과 가까워서 이 동네를 골랐어요.
There are several reasons, but above all I chose this neighborhood to be near family.
Everyday: highlights the decisive reason among many
새 직장은 무엇보다도 분위기가 좋아서 정말 마음에 들어요.
More than anything, I really like my new workplace because the atmosphere is good.
Real situation: 무엇보다도 points to the top factor in a personal judgment
nuance: 무엇보다 (literally 무엇 'what' + 보다 'than') is a fixed expression — 'than anything,' i.e. 'above all / more than anything' — that elevates one point over everything else, not just over one rival. It is the go-to way to mark your top priority or the most decisive factor when several are in play, and it pairs especially naturally with 중요하다. Adding -도 gives 무엇보다도, slightly more emphatic. Compare it with 특히 ('especially'), which merely spotlights a notable member of a group without ranking it first; 무엇보다 actively crowns one thing #1. It works in both speech and writing and feels warm and emphatic. The English-speaker pitfall is taking 보다 literally as a two-item comparison ('better than what?') and trying to name a single rival noun after it — 무엇보다 is frozen as 'above all,' comparing one point against the entire field, so don't parse it as 'than what' or expect a specific 'than X' object.

english: never; by no means (with a negative)
usage: never V; by no means V
Must be completed by a negative predicate — the core pattern
Very common with adjective + -지 않다 for emphatic denial
Pairs with 아니다 to firmly reject an identity or quality
결코 is more written/formal; 절대로 is the spoken everyday twin
examples: 저는 그 약속을 결코 잊지 않을 거예요.
I will never forget that promise.
Simple: 결코 demands the negative 잊지 않다 to land
이건 결코 쉬운 결정이 아니었어요.
This was by no means an easy decision.
Everyday: pairs with 아니다 to emphatically deny a quality
그분은 결코 그런 말을 할 사람이 아니에요.
He is by no means the kind of person who would say that.
Real situation: firmly defends someone by rejecting a possibility
nuance: 결코 is an emphatic negative adverb — 'never / by no means / not in the slightest' — and its defining rule is that it MUST co-occur with a negative ending such as -지 않다, 아니다, or 없다. It cannot stand alone or sit with a plain affirmative verb; the sentence feels broken without the negation. Its everyday partner is 절대(로): the two are close in meaning, but 결코 is more formal, written, and declaration-like (oaths, firm statements, editorials), while 절대로 is what you actually say out loud in conversation. 전혀 ('not at all') also negates but answers 'to what degree' (전혀 안 매워요), whereas 결코 conveys resolute 'never under any circumstances.' The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it onto English 'never,' which can stand in a positive-looking sentence ('I never go') — Korean 결코 cannot float free; you must supply the negative predicate, so 'I will never go' becomes '결코 가지 않을 거예요,' never '결코 갈 거예요.'

english: finally; at last; in the end
usage: Caps a long, drawn-out process with its awaited result
after a long N, at last
Common with achievement verbs to mark a hard-won success
마침내 is more literary/weighty; 드디어 is more spoken and excited
examples: 오래 기다린 소식이 마침내 도착했어요.
The long-awaited news finally arrived.
Simple: 마침내 frames the result as the end of a long wait
몇 년 동안 준비한 끝에 마침내 시험에 합격했어요.
After preparing for years, I finally passed the exam.
Everyday: '~ 끝에' supplies the long effort that 마침내 caps
여러 번 실패했지만 마침내 원하던 결과를 얻었어요.
I failed several times, but in the end I got the result I wanted.
Real situation: closes a struggle with the hard-won outcome
nuance: 마침내 (native Korean) means 'finally / at last' and frames an outcome as the culmination of a long process, sustained effort, or anxious wait — it carries the weight of something hard-won. Its everyday twin is 드디어: both mean 'finally,' but 드디어 is warmer, more spoken, and bursts with the speaker's excitement ('드디어 끝났다!'), while 마침내 is more literary, composed, and narrative — the word a novel or news report uses to crown a climax. A third cousin, 결국 ('in the end / after all'), can mark a neutral or even disappointing conclusion, whereas 마침내 implies the end was awaited and welcome. It loves the set-up '오랜 노력 끝에.' Two pitfalls for English speakers: don't use 마침내 for trivial 'and then finally' sequencing (just listing steps) — it promises a significant, awaited result — and don't confuse it with the look-alike 마침 ('as it happens / just in time'), e.g. '마침 너를 만났네,' which is about lucky coincidence, not culmination.

english: on the contrary; conversely; the other way around
usage: Links two opposite situations across sentences
to do it the other way around
Concrete physical sense: reversed manner or direction
오히려 strengthens it into 'no — the reverse, against expectation'
The 과/와 marks the specific reference point being reversed
examples: 형은 활발한데, 반대로 동생은 아주 조용해요.
The older brother is outgoing; conversely, the younger one is very quiet.
Simple: contrasts two people directly
쉬울 거라고 생각했는데 반대로 정말 어려웠어요.
I thought it would be easy, but on the contrary it was really hard.
Everyday: reverses the speaker's expectation
설명서와 반대로 조립해서 다시 해야 했어요.
I assembled it the opposite way from the manual, so I had to redo it.
Real situation: 'in the reverse manner,' with 과/와 naming the reference
nuance: 반대로 (Sino-Korean 反對, '反 anti/reverse + 對 face/oppose' → opposition) means 'the opposite way,' covering both 'on the contrary' (contrasting facts or expectations) and 'the other way around' (reversed manner or direction). Compare it with the connector 반면(에) ('whereas/on the other hand'): 반면(에) calmly sets two differing facts side by side ('도시는 편리한 반면 복잡해요'), while 반대로 points to an actual, literal opposite — a flipped action, a reversed direction, or an outcome contrary to what was expected. So 'the manual said left, I went right' is 반대로, but 'the city is convenient, whereas the countryside is quiet' is more naturally 반면에. When you reverse a specific reference, keep the 과/와: 설명서와 반대로, 예상과 반대로. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 반대로 as a neutral 'on the other hand' clause-linker where 반면(에) belongs — 반대로 specifically signals a true opposite, not merely a different angle.

Dropping the particle in 'N과/와 반대로' ('설명서 반대로'): when reversing a specific reference, the 과/와 is needed — 설명서와 반대로, 예상과 반대로.
Confusing it with 거꾸로: 거꾸로 is physically upside-down/backwards ('티셔츠를 거꾸로 입었어요'), while 반대로 is the broader 'opposite/conversely,' so 'wore it inside-out' is 거꾸로, not 반대로.

usage: Habitually closes with -만 to seal the exclusivity
solely for the sake of N
examples: 그동안 오로지 가족만 생각하며 일해 왔어요.
All this time I've worked thinking only of my family.
Simple: the -만 partner seals 'only family, nothing else'
이 결과는 오로지 본인의 노력 덕분이에요.
This result is entirely thanks to your own effort.
Everyday: attributes a cause to one factor alone
그 선수는 오로지 우승만을 목표로 몇 년을 훈련했어요.
That athlete trained for years aiming solely at the championship.
Real situation: 오로지 + 만을 marks one exclusive, all-consuming goal
nuance: 오로지 (native Korean) means 'only / solely / entirely' and emphasizes single-minded exclusivity — one purpose, one person, one cause, with everything else shut out. Its near-synonym is 오직, and both mean 'only,' but the dividing line is emotional temperature: 오직 is plainer and more matter-of-fact, while 오로지 carries a warmer, almost devotional weight, suggesting wholehearted dedication ('오로지 너만을 위해'). It naturally leans on -만 or -뿐 to complete the 'and nothing else' meaning. Crucially, 오로지 is about exclusive focus, not about small quantities — it is NOT the 'only/just X items' of counting. The English-speaker pitfall flows from that: English 'only' covers both devotion ('I think only of you') and scarcity ('only three left'), but Korean splits them — use 오로지/오직 for exclusive focus and 단지/겨우 for 'merely/only (so few),' so 'only three remain' is '겨우 세 개 남았어요,' never 오로지 세 개.

english: in a word; in short; to put it simply
usage: Sums the whole thing up with a single blunt label
to put it in one word
The fuller set form that explicitly announces a summary
Variant lead-in, slightly more 'let me be frank'
한마디로 is punchier, more spoken and opinionated
examples: 그 영화는 한마디로 시간 낭비였어요.
That movie was, in a word, a waste of time.
Simple: compresses a whole judgment into one phrase
한마디로 말하면, 준비가 부족했던 거예요.
To put it simply, we just weren't prepared enough.
Everyday: 말하면 leads into a blunt one-line summary
새 제도는 복잡해 보여도 한마디로 누구에게나 공평한 제도예요.
The new system may look complex, but in short it's one that's fair to everyone.
Real situation: cuts through detail to deliver the bottom line
nuance: 한마디로 (native Korean: 한 'one' + 마디 'a word/segment of speech' + -로 'by/in') means 'in a word / in short' and signals that you are about to condense everything into one blunt summary or label. It is conversational and usually evaluative — you reach for it right before dropping your bottom line, often a verdict ('한마디로 별로예요'). Compare it with the more neutral, businesslike 요약하면 ('to summarize'): 요약하면 sounds like minutes of a meeting, while 한마디로 sounds like a friend cutting to the chase with an opinion. Its fuller forms 한마디로 말하면 / 한마디로 말해서 are equally common. Two pitfalls for English speakers: don't follow 한마디로 with a long, multi-clause explanation — it literally promises ONE short takeaway, so keep what comes after crisp — and don't parse it word-for-word as 'with one word said'; it is a frozen discourse marker meaning 'in short / to sum up,' so the listener expects a punchy summary, not a literal single vocabulary word.
